title: Pixel to Geocoordinate UAV Mapping
fullTitle: Pixel to Geocoordinate Mapping in Oblique and Nadir UAV Imagery
summary: A practical pipeline bridging 2D pixel detections from nadir and oblique UAV drone imagery to high-precision 3D global geocoordinates (WGS84 GPS).
contentHtml:
Translating 2D pixel-level object detections from Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery into accurate 3D global geocoordinates (latitude, longitude, and elevation in WGS84) is a fundamental prerequisite for drone-based emergency response, wildfire tracking, search-and-rescue, and infrastructure inspection.


While nadir imagery (captured looking straight down at 90°) offers relatively uniform Ground Sample Distance (GSD), oblique imagery (captured at angles between 30° and 45°) provides critical lateral visibility for tree trunks, building facades, and steep terrains. However, oblique viewpoints introduce drastic perspective distortion, variable spatial footprints across the frame, altitude uncertainties, and orientation/gimbal sensor noise.


Methodology: End-to-End Georeferencing Pipeline


This paper presents a lightweight, computationally practical pipeline that achieves sub-11m geolocation accuracy without requiring exhaustive Structure-from-Motion (SfM) 3D point cloud reconstruction:

  • Camera Geometry & Collinearity Back-Projection: Combines calibrated camera intrinsics (focal length, principal point) and UAV extrinsic telemetry (GPS position, roll, pitch, yaw) to project pixel rays into world coordinates.
  • Digital Elevation Model (DEM) Sampling: Intersects projected rays with real-world topography rather than assuming a flat ground plane, eliminating elevation-induced horizontal parallax error.
  • Machine Learning Offset Correction Model: Trains a lightweight offset model on flight telemetry residuals to learn and eliminate systematic gimbal bias, sensor lag, and aerodynamic drift.

Empirical Evaluation


The system was tested extensively across 36 ground control targets under both nadir and oblique drone flights using five rigorous spatial metrics (geodesic distance using the Haversine formula, Circular Error Probable [CEP50], spatial error heatmaps, cluster compactness, and directional decomposition):

  • Raw flat-plane projection yielded an average geodesic error of 27.19 m.
  • Incorporating DEM elevation sampling reduced the average error to 20.21 m.
  • Deploying the machine learning offset model further reduced the mean error to 10.39 m with significantly tighter variance and lower CEP50.


*Note: This research was authored by Michal Aibin, Suchang Cao, Victor Wu, and Zhiyuan Yang, published in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP), pages 1–6.

title: Beyond sRGB - Color Space Wildfire Detection
fullTitle: Beyond sRGB: Optimizing Object Detection with Diverse Color Spaces for Precise Wildfire Risk Assessment
summary: Investigates diverse color spaces (Log RGB, Linear RGB, XYZ, LMS, D-Log) with vision transformers & YOLO11 for early wildfire risk detection, achieving +27.16% mAP.
contentHtml:
Forest fire risk assessment and early prevention are critical topics in environmental management and disaster mitigation. The predominant methodology relies on unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV/drone) imagery paired with deep learning-based object detection models. However, standard drone photography almost universally processes images into the sRGB color space through standard Image Signal Processing (ISP) pipelines.


While sRGB is optimized for human visual perception, its non-linear tone mapping and compression often strip away or compress subtle physical nuances—such as fine-grained light interactions with vegetation, canopy moisture loss, and dead wood—that are vital for computer vision algorithms tracking wildfire hazards.


Core Contributions & Methodology


In this research, we systematically investigate the impact of six distinct color spaces on state-of-the-art vision transformer models (such as CO-DETR and DDQ-DETR) and the latest convolutional detector (YOLO11) for tree condition and wildfire hazard detection:

  • Linear RGB: Preserves the direct physical linear interactions of light with natural forest surfaces before gamma compression.
  • Log RGB: Expands dynamic range and offers superior illumination invariance across changing environmental conditions and sunlight angles.
  • XYZ & LMS: Colorimetric and human cone-response representations decoupling luminance from chromatic components.
  • D-Log: Camera-native logarithmic profile preserving highlight and shadow details across broad sensor latitudes.

Quantitative Results & Impact


Our rigorous experiments demonstrate that alternative color spaces dramatically outperform conventional sRGB:

  • Log RGB achieved a 27.16% improvement in mean average precision ($ ext{mAP}_{50}$) over standard sRGB.
  • Log RGB delivered a 34.44% gain in mean average recall ($ ext{mAR}$), minimizing missed hazardous fuel targets.
  • Linear RGB also consistently outperformed sRGB, confirming that preserving radiometric linearity aids feature representations in deep networks.





*Note: This research was authored by Zhiyuan Yang, Suchang Cao, and Prof. Michał Aibin, published in MDPI Remote Sensing 17(9), 1503 (April 2025), cited by 10+.

Our goal is to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of solar panel farms mapping, advancing solar energy technology globally.

title: Airport Runway Insp.
summary: In the vast and challenging landscapes of northern Canada, where scattered communities heavily rely on air transportation for essential services, remote airp...
contentHtml:
In the vast and challenging landscapes of northern Canada, where scattered communities heavily rely on air transportation for essential services, remote airports face significant challenges such as limited resources, high operational costs, and logistical difficulties. The traditional manual inspection methods, plagued by infrequency, labor-intensity, and subjectivity, exacerbate these issues.


This paper proposes a novel solution utilizing modern technology, particularly drones equipped with advanced sensors and computer vision. The project aims to collect precise baseline data from the 117 remote airports in Canada, 94 of which have gravel runways, to enhance safety and infrastructure longevity. The drones will capture high-resolution imagery, and computer vision analysis will be applied to detect runway defects, vegetation issues, and potential hazards for proactive maintenance, presenting a promising approach to address these longstanding challenges in remote airport management.



*Note: This research project is leaded by Prof. Michal Aibin and Prof. Lino Coria Mendoza from Northeastern University, and supported by TransCanada and Spexi Geospatial.

title: Forest Fire Risk Eval.
fullTitle: Forest Fire Risk Assessment with Deep Learning Methods and UAV Imagery
summary: "Canada is having its worst fire season in modern history. The fires have burnt more than 20 million acres, casting hazardous smoke over parts of the U.S. an...
contentHtml:
"Canada is having its worst fire season in modern history. The fires have burnt more than 20 million acres, casting hazardous smoke over parts of the U.S. and stretching Canadian firefighting resources thin." [NPR]


Once a fire starts, it becomes extremely challenging to extinguish. The most efficient approach to minimizing losses is by preventing fires from occurring in the first place. Unfortunately, existing systems lack the capability to accurately predict fires. Moreover, traditional monitoring methods have limitations in terms of coverage range, cost, and maintenance.


To address these challenges, this research proposes an innovative end-to-end forest fire risk assessment system that combines the YOLOv8 object detection algorithm, UAV imagery, and visualization techniques. This system effectively assesses the risk of forest fires and presents the information in a user-friendly manner for a wider audience.





*Note: This research project is leaded by Prof. Michal Aibin and Prof. Lino Coria Mendoza from Northeastern University, and supported by TransCanada and Spexi Geospatial.

title: AR Image Tracking
summary: Augmented Reality (AR) is an innovative technology capable of superimposing virtual information onto the real-world environment, offering immense potential a...
contentHtml:
Augmented Reality (AR) is an innovative technology capable of superimposing virtual information onto the real-world environment, offering immense potential and value across various industries and in our daily lives. Despite its promise, AR's widespread adoption remains in its early stages due to hardware limitations and the complexity of improving algorithms. This paper delves into a critical component of AR image tracking—the keypoint detection algorithm. This algorithm marks the initial and vital step in AR applications. As image tracking operates in real-time and real-world scenarios, the algorithms must exhibit exceptional qualities, including high speed, accuracy, and resilience to variations and noise.


Our study examines both traditional handcrafted keypoint detection algorithms, such as SIFT, SURF, ORB, and cutting-edge deep learning algorithms like SuperPoint, in the context of AR image tracking scenarios. By conducting rigorous tests and comparisons, we aim to identify the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Additionally, we will address the best practices when implementing AR image tracking using keypoint detection algorithms.

title: Not Hotdog App
summary: Not Hog Dog Project is inspired by the great HBO show Silicon Valley. In one of the episodes, Jian-Yang was tasked to build an app that’d use AI to recognize...
contentHtml:
Not Hog Dog Project is inspired by the great HBO show Silicon Valley. In one of the episodes, Jian-Yang was tasked to build an app that’d use AI to recognize food pictures and correctly label them. On the demo day, the app seemed to begin working perfectly without a glitch and labeled a newly-taken picture as “hot dog”. But as other types of food pictures were attempted, the app was only able to label the rest of them as “not hot dog”...


The objective of this project is to create an application identical to the one demonstrated in the show. Our approach involves several key steps:

  • Model Training: We will commence by training two Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models, YOLOv5 and ResNet152 using a carefully curated Hotdog dataset. This dataset will serve as the foundation for teaching the models to recognize and differentiate hotdog images accurately.
  • Model Deployment: Once the CNN models are trained, we will select the best-performing model and deploy it on a server. This step ensures that the model's capabilities are accessible over the internet and can be utilized by the web app.
  • Web App Development: The next phase involves building a user-friendly web application that connects to the server. This web app will allow users to upload images or use their camera to capture pictures. The uploaded images will then be processed by the deployed model to determine whether they contain hotdogs or not.

True Positive Rate 90.16% 98.4%

title: Trip Planner
summary: My friend Jack is planning a trip to Vancouver for the winter break vacation with his girlfriend. Their flight to YVR is on Saturday night, December 17th. Th...
contentHtml:
Real Life Problem


My friend Jack is planning a trip to Vancouver for the winter break vacation with his girlfriend. Their flight to YVR is on Saturday night, December 17th. They have already booked a hotel that they believe is cheap, convenient, and of good quality - the Century Plaza Hotel, located in the center of Downtown Vancouver. They decided to rent a car to transition from place to place during the trip to save time and have access to more distant locations. They have selected six places to visit in Vancouver after conducting their research. The six places are as follows:

  1. Granville Island
  2. Stanley Park
  3. Lynn Canyon Park
  4. Queen Elizabeth Park
  5. Cypress Mountain
  6. Golden Ears

They need a route plan that can shorten their overall trip time. However, there are certain rules they must follow:

  1. They must stay at the Century Plaza Hotel throughout the entire trip; switching to other hotels is not allowed.
  2. They want to visit all six places, without missing any or adding extra ones.
  3. Each place can only be visited once; no repeated visits are allowed.
  4. Every day's trip must start and end at the hotel.
  5. They only have 6 hours each day for visiting, as they don't want the trip to be exhausting.
  6. If the trip of a day takes less than 6 hours and it is not the last day, it will still be counted as a 6-hour trip.
  7. The last day's trip will be counted with the actual hours spent.
  8. Currently, they don't need to consider the business hours of each place.

With the above rules in mind, they need to create the best route plan for the whole trip.


Data Preparation


We collected the transition time data and staying time data from Google Maps App. We then summarized the data in the following chart (A-G represent the six places):

Visiting Time (Transition Time + Staying Time)
Time (hour) A B C D E F G
A - 3.25 3.1 2.5 1.3 4.6 3.4
B 0.25 - 3.3 2.6 1.25 4.8 3.2
C 0.2 3.4 - 2.3 1.5 4.4 3.2
D 0.6 3.7 3.5 - 1.6 4.5 3.1
E 0.3 3.25 3.4 2.5 - 4.75 3.1
F 0.8 4 3.5 2.6 1.9 - 3.5
G 1.2 4.2 4.2 3.0 2.1 5.3 -


Methodology and Result


The algorithms we researched include Brute force (DFS and BFS), Greedy, and Dijkstra, which we learned from CS5800. Additionally, we delved further into some potential Artificial Intelligence Algorithms, including Hill-Climbing Algorithm, Random Restart Hill-Climbing, A-star Algorithm, and Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) Algorithm. All these algorithms can solve this problem successfully. However, their performances vary.


Algorithm Comparison
Algorithm Optimal Solution Run Time Implementation Difficulty Time Complexity Space Complexity
Brute Force Y 48.0 Easy O(n!) O(n!)
Greedy N 0.26 Medium O(n2) O(n)
Dijkstra Y 61.5 Medium O(bd) O(n!)
Hill-Climb N 2.9 Easy O(inf.) O(n)
Random Restart N 27.7 Easy O(inf.) O(n)
A-star Y 47.8 Hard O(bd) O(n!)
CSP Y N/A Hard N/A N/A

The Greedy algorithm is the fastest among these 7 algorithms. It can help us obtain a good solution, but not necessarily an optimal one. The Hill-Climbing Algorithm is the second fastest algorithm. It did find the optimal solution for our real-life problem example, but it cannot guarantee to always find the optimal solution. Random Restart Hill-Climbing can improve the solution if the problem is complicated, but it also cannot guarantee to find the optimal solution, even with infinite restarts.


The main ideas of A-star and Dijkstra are very similar. They both use greedy methods to extend the search and are capable of finding the optimal solution. A-star's performance is better than Dijkstra, while Dijkstra's implementation is slightly simpler than A-star. Breadth-first search and depth-first search are the worst in terms of performance. However, both of them guarantee to find an optimal solution, and DFS has better space complexity than BFS.


*Note: This is a group project collaborated with my teammates Xilong Cai and Fangxiao Guo.

This tutorial is a culmination of Mr. Liao Xuefeng's 2016 Python 3 tutorial, and enriched with the latest frontend technologies. Instead of relying on established and convenient Python web development frameworks like Flask or Django, this tutorial takes a ground-up approach, guiding readers through building a web application from scratch.


The tutorial covers a wide range of topics, starting with setting up the database, constructing the web framework, implementing the ORM (Object-Relational Mapping), establishing the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern, creating APIs, and finally crafting frontend pages using CSS/HTML, JavaScript, and DOM manipulation. title: Time Traveler VR
summary: The landscape process exerts a slow, silent, yet powerful impact on our world and daily lives. As contemporary humans, immersed in the struggles of the prese...
contentHtml:
The landscape process exerts a slow, silent, yet powerful impact on our world and daily lives. As contemporary humans, immersed in the struggles of the present, it becomes incredibly challenging for us to grasp the significance of past events or foresee the implications for the future. Here, the role of a landscape architect becomes crucial, as they serve as communicators and advocates, drawing attention to these issues for the public's awareness.


In this context, virtual reality emerges as a groundbreaking design medium, offering unique qualities that have the potential to effectively convey such complex problems compared to traditional media. This project aims to explore the possibilities of interpreting the landscape process through innovative means, leveraging immersive virtual environments and first-person storytelling.


By harnessing the power of virtual reality, the project seeks to create a profound and engaging experience for users, enabling them to comprehend the profound impacts of landscape processes in a more tangible and immersive manner. Through this novel approach, the project aspires to raise awareness, foster a deeper understanding of our environment, and encourage positive actions toward sustainable and responsible site development.








*Note: This is a Landscape Architecture Thesis Project instructed by Prof. Robyn Reed.
